Development of public land use within the Desert Renewable Energy Conservation Plan (DRECP) boundary is taking place through collaboration of the California Energy Commission (CEC), the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (USFWS), the California Department of Fish and Wildlife (CDFW) and the U.S. Bureau of Land Management (USBLM) in order to 1) identify areas of land with high-quality renewable energy potential and 2) provide for the long-term conservation and management of endangered and threatened species as well as areas of biological, physical, cultural and social importance. Home to threatened, endangered and protected (TEP) species, endemic lineages and evolutionary hotspots, the desert biota face widespread threats (e.g. human development, subsidized predation, linear corridors, off-highway vehicles, military training, invasive plants, climate change, and renewable energy).
Privately owned land existing within the DRECP provides potential opportunities for private environmental organizations to expand on federal and state landscape-scale conservation efforts. I will be showcasing a spatially explicit decision support system (DSS) that was built to help a private environmental organization identify parcels to target for land acquisition, conservation, and restoration. Differing from others in its versatility and its weighting scheme, this DSS works under differing conservation scenarios (e.g. conservation vs restoration) and includes nonlinear weighting of criterion (attribute) values, providing more flexibility to the decision maker when assigning weights to evaluation criteria.

THE GRADUATE SCHOOL

We recommend that the thesis prepared under our supervision by **Courtney Butt** entitled **Desert Conservation Priorities Mapping Tool** be accepted in partial fulfillment of the requirements for the degree of **Master of Science** Kenneth Nussear, Ph.D. _Advisor_ Scott Bassett, Ph.D. Co _mmittee Member_ Kyra Stull, Ph.D. _Graduate School Representative_ Markus Kemmelmeier, Ph.D., Dean _Graduate School_ August, 2024

## ABSTRACT

Development of public land use within the Desert Renewable Energy

Conservation Plan (DRECP) boundary is taking place through collaboration of the

California Energy Commission (CEC), the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (USFWS), the California Department of Fish and Wildlife (CDFW) and the U.S. Bureau of Land

Management (USBLM) in order to 1) identify areas of land with high-quality renewable energy potential and 2) provide for the long-term conservation and management of endangered and threatened species as well as areas of biological, physical, cultural and social importance. The DRECP covers 22,585,000 acres of southern California, encompassing the Mojave and Colorado Deserts. Home to threatened, endangered and protected (TEP) species, endemic lineages and evolutionary hotspots, the desert biota face widespread threats (e.g. human development, subsidized predation, linear corridors, off-highway vehicles, military training, invasive plants, climate change, and renewable energy). Privately owned land existing within the DRECP provides potential opportunities for private environmental organizations to expand on federal and state landscape-scale conservation efforts. I will be showcasing a spatially explicit decision support system (DSS) that was built to help a private environmental organization identify parcels to target for land acquisition, conservation, and restoration. Differing from others in its versatility and its weighting scheme, this DSS works under differing conservation

scenarios (e.g. conservation vs restoration) and includes nonlinear weighting of criterion

(attribute) values, providing more flexibility to the decision maker when assigning weights to evaluation criteria.

## SECTION 1: INTRODUCTION

- 1.1 Mojave Desert Land Trust Agreement

The Mojave Desert Land Trust (MDLT) is an accredited land trust located in

Joshua Tree, California. Their mission is to protect the Colorado and Mojave Desert ecosystems, and their natural, cultural and scenic resources. To date, MDLT has procured 110,000 acres across the California deserts and within national parks, national

monuments, wilderness areas, and habitat linkages between them (Research Agreement 2022). The Mojave Desert Land Trust aims to purchase 100,000 acres over the next five years with a focus on protecting ecologically important land in desert wildlife corridors and climate refugia, in hopes of helping meet the larger picture of maintaining an interconnected ecosystem throughout the southern California deserts (Research Agreement 2022). MDLT recognizes the need for a mapping tool (i.e. decision support system) to assist them in prioritizing areas for land acquisition, restoration and conservation. They requested the mapping tool focus on the area within the Desert Renewable Energy Conservation Plan (DRECP) boundary, with an added 20 km buffer surrounding the DRECP boundary (conversation with Kelly Herbinson, Execute Director of MDLT 2/15/23) (Figure 1). Other groups (Penrod et al. 2012) have mapped the conservation value within this region or are in the process of mapping the area (BLM through Conservation Science Partners and California Natural Resources Agency for

30x30) but not to the extent or fine-scale they desire (Research Agreement 2022). MDLT requested the following data be included within the desert conservation priorities mapping tool:

1. Springs, aquifers, waterways and/or other water features

2. Development threat level

3. Development focus areas

4. Critical habitat for sensitive, rare, and/or protected species

5. Biodiversity and/or species richness

6. Habitat linkages between already protected wilderness areas (National Parks,

Monuments, Wilderness Areas)

7. Wildlife corridors for ecologically important, rare, or representative species 8. Climate refugia for target species (western Joshua trees and others) 9. Carbon sequestration- active or potential 10. Other ecologically significant areas 11. Areas of historic or cultural value 12. Parcel information MDLT requested the mapping tool be interactive, giving them control in choosing which data layers to focus on based on their objective (e.g. conservation vs restoration). The mapping tool must also include a downloadable map for external viewing, based on user data layer choices (Research Agreement 2022).

Figure 1. The study area consists of the Desert Renewable Energy Conservation Plan Boundary with a 20 km buffer, encompassing the Mojave and Colorado D eserts of southern California and portions of Nevada and Arizona. 1.2 Conservation Value The Mojave and Colorado Deserts of southern California are home to multiple threatened, endangered and protected (TEP) species (Table 1), endemic lineages (e.g. Mojave Desert Tortoise and Mohave Ground Squirrel) and ecological hotspots (Figure 2). Ecological threats due to human development (Averill-Murray et al. 2013), subsidized predation (Esque et al. 2010), linear corridors (Vandergast et al. 2013), off-highway vehicles (Carter et al. 2020), military training (Doe et al. 2014), invasive species (Drake et al. 2016), climate change (Ackerly et al. 2010) and renewable energy development (Agha et al. 2020) abound within California’s desert landscape. The use of the desert conservation priorities mapping tool by the Mojave Desert Land Trust will provide

opportunities for the protection and restoration of ecosystems as well as the natural,

cultural and scenic resources found within southern California’s desert habitat.

- 1.3 Thesis Objectives and Outcomes

The purpose of this thesis is to create a spatially explicit, user-driven mapping tool for the Mojave Desert Land Trust (MDLT) that serves as a guide in prioritizing the purchase of land according to changeable objectives. In order to meet the requirements of the MDLT, the desert conservation priorities mapping tool was built as a decision support system (DSS) that (1) provides numerous scenarios to accommodate for differences in conservation priorities, (2) ranks the conservation value of land within the study area based on numerous evaluation criteria and (3) leads to the identification of land parcels that MDLT can target for land acquisition, restoration, and conservation. With these outcomes in mind, the two objectives for my thesis were to build a DSS that (1) expresses the evaluation criteria in a meaningful way so they can be used to answer multiple conservation questions and (2) employs a simple, yet versatile weighting scheme, allowing the user to assign weights to the evaluation criteria based on their conservation priorities. My approach to the first objective was to allow the same input features (i.e. evaluation criteria) to be considered in different contexts (e.g. positive versus negative impacts) depending on the goal of the scenario. For example - distanceto-roads or disturbance could be considered negative when the goal is to preserve habitat for a species, but in a restoration context - this may be land that is desirable to acquire. My approach to meeting the second objective was to allow the user to assign weights to each evaluation criterion in a simple, flexible way in order to best meet their objective. The desert conservation priorities mapping tool employs a combination rule, where the user assigns two weights to each evaluation criteria. For the first weight, they use a direct rating method to designate the relative importance of the evaluation criteria to the

objective. For the second weight, the user will scale the attributes of each evaluation criterion either linearly or nonlinearly. The option of weighting the data nonlinearly adds greater flexibility to the DSS by permitting the user to give a stronger weighting

influence to specific values within the evaluation criteria. For instance, if the user was looking to purchase parcels to help with the conservation of amphibians (e.g. Arroyo

toad), the user could give a stronger weight to areas closer to water within the Distance to water data layer.

This mapping tool is an interesting expansion of a typical DSS because it is multipurpose and provides added flexibility when designating the criterion (attribute) value weights. Not commonly seen, the added option to scale the evaluation (attribute) criteria nonlinearly sets the desert conservation priorities mapping tool apart. SECTION 2: LITERATURE REVIEW 2.1 The Mojave and Colorado Deserts of Southern California The Mojave and Colorado Deserts of southern California are the most arid ecosystems found in North America (Garfin et al. 2013, Hereford et al. 2006, Lovich et al. 2023) occupying portions of the Imperial, Inyo, Kern, Los Angeles, Riverside, San Bernardino and San Diego counties. According to oral tradition, the Cahuilla,

Chemehuevi, Kawaiisu, Mojave, Serrano and Southern Paiutes have inhabited portions of

this land since time immemorial (Laird 1974; Smith et al. 2022). Supporting this, the

archeological record shows evidence of humans residing in the Mojave since the Late

Pleistocene (Sutton 1996). When European explorers arrived in the area, the

Chemehuevi, Kawaiisu, and Serrano groups were occupying portions of the central

Mojave Desert. The Serrano group kept a semi-sedentary lifestyle and had villages along the Mojave River with a population up to 80 people or more. In contrast, the Chemehuevi and Kawaiisu had smaller populations, were more mobile, and were spread out over

larger areas of land (Earle 2005). Altogether, the impact of indigenous people on the land was minimal and localized (Leu et al. 2008). Land-use intensity increased with the arrival of European explorers in the mid-16th century and continued when the United States acquired the land in the mid-1800s. Initial expeditions through the California Deserts were made by explorers and early settlers, (USBLM 1980) followed by a steady influx of immigrants arriving from foreign countries, coastal southern California, and the midwestern United States (Norris 1982). By 1868, most of the major land uses of the area were for livestock grazing, mining, military bases, transportation (e.g. railroads), and urban growth (USBLM 1980). Homesteading, in relatively isolated pockets of the desert, emerged in the early 1870s but was abandoned within fifty years due to short and longlived periods of drought (Norris 1982). In the 1930s, water projects (e.g. Colorado River Aqueduct) brought pumping stations to the area along with the introduction of long, highvoltage power transmission lines (USBLM 1980). The production of paved roads also came in the 1930s and by the 1960s and 1970s interstate highways were in place (Nystrom 2003; Smith et al. 2022). Alongside all these advances, California’s population experienced a 1,750% growth increase over the twentieth century, growing from two million to thirty-five million people (Gomben et al. 2012). By 2020, California’s population had reached 39.5 million (U.S. Census Bureau 2020). With continued

population growth, human land use within the Mojave and Colorado Deserts of southern California has steadily expanded (Leu et al. 2008).

In response to growth in land use, a number of conservation efforts were made in the twentieth century. In the 1930s, the Anza-Borrego State Park and Joshua Tree and Death Valley National Monuments (later National Parks) were established. In 1976, the California Desert Conservation Area (CDCA) (Figure 3) was designated through the Federal Land Policy and Management Act (FLPMA) for the purpose of administration and protection of public lands and its resources (USBLM 1980). Part of this management plan included designating land for energy development. The southern California Deserts are replete with wind and geothermal energy resources and offer the insolation and land requirements for large-scale solar energy projects (Dritschilo et al. 1986). Multiple federal (e.g. 2005 Energy Policy Act) and state (e.g. California Executive Order S-14-08) laws and policies calling for increased energy production from renewable resources heightened the interest of renewable energy projects on public and private lands within the area. The 2005 Energy Policy Act established a minimum goal of 10,000 megawatts of renewable energy generation on public lands to take place within the next 10 years. The California Executive Order S-14-08, signed by Governor Schwarzeneggar in 2008, mandated 33% of California’s energy production come from renewable energy by 2020 (USBLM 2016). Seeing the interest in renewable energy development, and recognizing the need to

protect threatened and endangered species and areas of recreational and cultural

significance within the Mojave and Colorado Deserts, the California Energy

Commission, the California Department of Fish and Wildlife, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and the U.S. Bureau of Land Management (i.e. DRECP partner agencies) came together in 2008 to initiate a planning effort of public and private land within the area. In

2009 this collaborative effort was formalized and in 2010 the DRECP partner agencies signed the Desert Renewable Energy Conservation Plan (DRECP) Planning Agreement (USBLM 2016). This federal and state landscape-scale planning effort covers 22,585,000 acres of southern California within the Mojave and Colorado Deserts (Figure 4), and includes most of the CDCA. The goals of the DRECP partner agencies are two-fold. The first is to identify specific areas of land that have high-quality renewable energy potential in order to meet the federal and state renewable energy targets and policies, while also

providing access to transmission lines where the environmental impact can be managed and mitigated (USBLM 2016). Their second goal is to provide for the long-term conservation and management of threatened and endangered species as well as other areas of biological, physical, cultural, scenic or social importance within the DRECP boundary (Kreiter 2015; USBLM 2016). In 2009, President Obama signed the Omnibus Act, congressionally establishing the National Landscape Conservation System (NLCS) to “conserve, protect, and restore nationally significant landscapes that have outstanding cultural, ecological, and scientific values for the benefit of current and future generations” (USBLM 2016). As such, public lands within the CDCA administered by the BLM for conservation purposes were incorporated into the NLCS. In 2014, the DRECP partner agencies published the Draft DRECP, which included their plans to achieve their renewable energy and conservation goals. In 2015, after a 152-day public comment period for the document, the DRECP partner agencies announced the completion of the plan would follow a phased approach in order to allow them to work with California counties (USBLM 2016).
